stories.title: Does Organic Mean No Pesticides?
alternates: What Organic Farmers Are Allowed to Spray
Organic Pesticides: Fewer, Mostly Milder, Not All Harmless
stories.question: Does organic farming really mean no pesticides, and are the ones it uses safer?
stories.whyWatch: Many shoppers pay for organic believing nothing was sprayed. The organic rulebook says otherwise, and the EU's hazard classifications show how the pesticides organic farms may use compare with the rest.
stories.tension: Dozens of videos say organic means pesticide-free; sceptics answer that organic pesticides are no safer than synthetic ones. The rules show organic farms do spray, and the hazard data show the organic list is mostly milder, with two real exceptions.
stories.evidenceNeeded: The organic regulation's own rules on pest control and its list of allowed synthetic substances, the EU count of pesticides approved for organic use, and their hazard classifications against all approved pesticides.

stories.premise: Organic farming does use pesticides. US rules (7 CFR 205.206) let organic producers apply biological, botanical or National List substances when preventive practices fail, and 7 CFR 205.601 lists synthetic ones among them, such as insecticidal soaps, horticultural oils, lime sulfur and copper fungicides. In the EU, 26 of 385 authorised pesticide substances are also approved for organic farming, plus two synthetic pyrethroids allowed only in insect traps. That list is mostly of low concern: 10 of the 26 have any identified toxicity, against 340 of all 385, and none is classed as a suspected carcinogen or reproductive toxicant (27 and 26 among all approved). The exceptions are real: pyrethrins act like synthetic pyrethroids, and copper is toxic at high intakes and harmful to aquatic life. These are EU hazard classes, not measured exposure or harm, and the US list differs.

arc.conflict: The sources do not agree, and both sides have a case.
arc.evidence: Lay the studies side by side (USDA organic regulations (7 CFR 205), Mie 2017 review, health effects of organic food and farming, Baranski 2014 meta-analysis, organic crops): design, sample, what was measured.
arc.resolution: Organic is a short list of pesticides used after prevention, mostly natural and mostly of low concern, with a few synthetic exceptions and two natural ones, pyrethrins and copper, that are not harmless; it is not pesticide-free farming.
arc.takeaway: The conditions under which the claim holds, instead of a yes or no.

coherence.explanation: One question, what does organic farming spray: the rule that organic farms may apply approved substances when prevention fails, the fact that the approved list includes some synthetics, and how hazardous that list is. Shoppers who believe organic means pesticide-free are asking whether it is safe, so the hazard comparison is part of the same answer.

alternates: What the Studies Show About Organic Food and Your Health
Organic Food's Health Benefits: Proven or Assumed?
stories.question: Does eating organic food actually make you healthier?
stories.whyWatch: Health is the main reason people pay more for organic. Several systematic reviews looked for the benefit in people, not in the food, and agree on what is and is not known.
stories.tension: Organic eaters do show lower rates of obesity, allergies and some cancers in observational studies, and many videos treat that as proof. The reviews say those people also eat and live differently, and the few trials are short and measure surrogate markers.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Systematic reviews of human studies on organic diets and health outcomes, with their assessment of confounding and trial quality.

Mie 2017 review, health effects of organic food and farming: wrong (0.6, direct)

Srednicka-Tober 2016 meta-analysis, organic milk: wrong (0.35, direct)
Srednicka-Tober 2016 meta-analysis, organic meat: wrong (0.3, direct)
Winter and Katz 2011, dietary risk on Dirty Dozen produce: wrong (0.25, direct)

stories.premise: No health benefit of eating organic is proven. A 2019 systematic review of 35 studies found observational links with lower metabolic syndrome, obesity, non-Hodgkin lymphoma and other outcomes, but organic eaters also eat more plants and live healthier lives, trials were short and measured surrogate markers, and the evidence does not allow a definitive statement of long-term benefit. A 2017 review reached the same conclusion, the Stanford review found only 3 of 17 human studies examined clinical outcomes, with no differences, and the American Academy of Pediatrics found no well-powered human study showing benefit. Not proven is not the same as shown to be absent: the one consistent finding is lower pesticide levels in urine.

stories.title: Does Organic Farming Grow Less Food?
alternates: The Organic Yield Gap, Measured
How Much Less Does an Organic Field Produce?
stories.question: Does organic farming really grow less food?
stories.whyWatch: Whether organic can feed the world turns on one number, how much less an organic field yields. A meta-analysis of more than a thousand comparisons puts a figure on it, and explains why some reports call the yields comparable.
stories.tension: A pediatric clinical report says well-designed studies show organic yields comparable to conventional; a meta-analysis of 115 studies across 38 countries finds a consistent gap for every crop type.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Meta-analyses of side-by-side organic and conventional yields, with their confidence intervals and the reasons the gap varies.
evidenceAvailable: Ponisio 2015 meta-analysis, organic yield gap: right (0.75, direct)
Mie 2017 review, health effects of organic food and farming: right (0.3, direct)
AAP 2012 clinical report on organic foods, abstract: wrong (0.25, direct)
gaps: What explains the split between Ponisio 2015 meta-analysis, organic yield gap, Mie 2017 review, health effects of organic food and farming, AAP 2012 clinical report on organic foods, abstract?
stories.premise: The weight of evidence says organic yields less, by less than often claimed. Ponisio and colleagues pooled 1,071 comparisons from 115 studies in 38 countries and found organic yields 19.2% lower (95% credible interval 15.5 to 22.9%), with conventional ahead for every crop type, a smaller gap than earlier meta-analyses, and they note publication bias may overstate it. A 2017 review adds that organic yields are typically limited by nitrogen. The dissent is a one-sentence summary in the American Academy of Pediatrics abstract that well-designed studies show comparable yields, not a yield analysis of its own.

arc.conflict: The studies do not agree, and both sides have a case.
arc.evidence: Lay the studies side by side (Ponisio 2015 meta-analysis, organic yield gap, Mie 2017 review, health effects of organic food and farming, AAP 2012 clinical report on organic foods, abstract): design, sample, what was measured.
arc.resolution: About a fifth less on average, consistently across crops; the comparable-yield claim rests on a single summary sentence, not on the pooled data.
arc.takeaway: The conditions under which the claim holds, instead of a yes or no.

stories.title: Does Eating Organic Cut Your Pesticide Intake?
alternates: What Happens to Pesticide Levels When You Switch to Organic
Organic Produce Has Fewer Residues, but Not Zero
stories.question: Does eating organic actually lower the pesticides you take in?
stories.whyWatch: Lower pesticide exposure is the most common reason people buy organic. Food monitoring and diet-switch trials measure it directly, and the effect is large and fast, while the health payoff is a separate, open question.
stories.tension: Organic produce is sold as residue-free, and sceptics say the difference is trivial. Monitoring finds residues on organic food too, yet people's urinary pesticide levels drop sharply within days of switching.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Residue monitoring that compares organic and conventional samples, and diet intervention trials that measure pesticide metabolites in urine before and after switching.
evidenceAvailable: Vigar 2019 systematic review, organic diet and health: right (0.75, direct)
Mie 2017 review, health effects of organic food and farming: right (0.5, direct)
Hyland 2019 organic diet intervention, abstract: right (0.45, direct)
Smith-Spangler 2012 review (Stanford), abstract: right (0.4, direct)
Mie 2017 review, health effects of organic food and farming: right (0.6, direct)
Smith-Spangler 2012 review (Stanford), abstract: right (0.5, direct)
Clark and Tilman 2017, environmental impacts of farming systems: right (0.25, direct)
Baranski 2014 meta-analysis, organic crops: right (0.65, partial)
Winter and Katz 2011, dietary risk on Dirty Dozen produce: right (0.55, partial)
stories.premise: Yes, by a lot, though not to zero. EU monitoring found quantifiable residues in 43.7% of all samples against 13.8% of organic ones, and a meta-analysis found detectable residues on 46% of conventional and 11% of organic crops, though few studies compared concentrations; US monitoring summarised by Winter and Katz still found residues on 23% of organic samples. Whole-diet switch trials in children and adults cut urinary pesticide metabolites, by up to 90%, within a few days. These are exposure measures; whether the lower exposure improves health is not established here.

arc.hook: Swap a family's food to organic for a week and measure what comes out in their urine.
arc.conflict: The claims pulling in different directions: "Organic produce carries lower pesticide residues than conventional produce"; "Switching to an organic diet quickly lowers pesticide levels in the body"; "Pesticide residues on conventional produce are too low to harm health"; "Organic farming uses no pesticides"; "Pesticides allowed in organic farming are not necessarily safer than synthetic ones"; "The Dirty Dozen list is a reliable guide to which produce to buy organic"; "Washing produce removes most pesticide residue".
arc.evidence: Each claim's verdict, strongest study first.
arc.resolution: Eating organic sharply lowers pesticide residues on your food and in your body, but organic food is not residue-free, and less exposure is not the same as a proven health benefit.
arc.takeaway: A decision rule the viewer can apply.

coherence.explanation: Pruned to one question, does eating organic lower the pesticides you take in: residues on organic versus conventional produce, and what happens to urinary pesticide levels when people switch. Whether conventional residues harm health, the Dirty Dozen and washing are separate questions with their own candidates, and the pesticide-use claims belong to the organic-farming story.

stories.question: What does the USDA organic seal actually guarantee?
stories.whyWatch: The organic seal is one of the few food labels backed by a detailed federal rule. Reading that rule answers what shoppers argue about: how much of the product is organic, whether GMOs and antibiotics are allowed, whether organic beef is grass-fed, and whether imported organic follows the same rule.
stories.tension: Shoppers assume organic means 100% organic, grass-fed and the same rule everywhere. The rule sets a 95% floor for the seal and a 70% floor for 'made with organic', lets organic cattle be finished on grain, and accepts some imports under foreign standards judged equivalent.
stories.evidenceNeeded: The text of the federal organic regulation on product composition, excluded methods, livestock health care and feeding, the USDA's own summary, and the Inspector General's audit of import equivalence arrangements.

stories.premise: The seal guarantees specific, checkable things. A product labelled organic must contain at least 95% organic ingredients by weight, excluding water and salt; 'made with organic' needs only 70% and may not carry the seal. Organic products must be made without genetic engineering, and no animal treated with antibiotics, nor its milk or meat, may be sold as organic, nor may hormones be given for growth (a sick animal must still be treated, and then loses organic status). The seal does not mean grass-fed: organic ruminants must graze in the grazing season, but slaughter stock are typically grain finished, in feedlots for up to a fifth of their life or 120 days, and EU organic diets may include up to 40% concentrate. Imports are certified either to the USDA rule or under equivalence arrangements with partners such as Canada, the EU and Japan, which need be equivalent, not identical: the Inspector General's 2017 audit counted dozens of procedural and technical differences in two arrangements without documented resolution of all of them. That audit predates the 2023 enforcement rule and measured no fraud rate.

arc.hook: Pick up three boxes labelled 100% organic, organic and made with organic, and ask what each promises.
arc.conflict: The claims pulling in different directions: "The USDA Organic seal requires at least 95 percent organic ingredients"; "Products labelled "made with organic" ingredients need only 70 percent organic content"; "USDA Organic prohibits genetically engineered ingredients"; "Organic livestock cannot be given antibiotics or added growth hormones"; "Organic beef and dairy can come from grain-fed animals"; "Organic produce may legally carry synthetic pesticide residues up to a small fraction of the legal tolerance"; "The "natural" label has little regulatory meaning"; "Hormones are banned in all US poultry and pork, so a "no hormones" label on them adds nothing".
arc.evidence: Each claim's verdict, strongest study first.
arc.resolution: The seal is a real rule: 95% organic content, no genetic engineering, no antibiotics or growth hormones; it is not a promise of grass-fed beef, and an imported product may meet an equivalent foreign standard rather than the identical US one.
arc.takeaway: A decision rule the viewer can apply.

coherence.explanation: Pruned to one question, what does the USDA organic seal guarantee: the 95% and 70% tiers, the genetic-engineering ban, the antibiotics and hormones rule, the grain-feeding allowance, and whether imports carrying the seal meet the same rule. The 'natural' and poultry-hormone claims are about other labels, and the residue tolerance belongs with the pesticide stories.

stories.title: Is Organic Food More Nutritious?
alternates: What Is Actually Different Inside Organic Food
More Omega-3, More Polyphenols: What Organic Food Contains
stories.question: Is organic food more nutritious than conventional food?
stories.whyWatch: Videos either say organic is packed with more nutrients or that it is identical. Large meta-analyses find something more specific: a few real differences, in particular compounds, with no proven effect on health.
stories.tension: Sceptics cite reviews finding no meaningful nutritional difference; advocates cite meta-analyses finding far more antioxidants and omega-3. Both are right about different things.
stories.evidenceNeeded: Meta-analyses of composition differences in organic crops, milk and meat, with their reliability ratings and what the authors say about health relevance.
evidenceAvailable: Srednicka-Tober 2016 meta-analysis, organic milk: right (0.75, direct)
Mie 2017 review, health effects of organic food and farming: right (0.65, direct)

stories.premise: Organic food differs in a few specific compounds, not across the board. A meta-analysis of 170 studies found about 56% more omega-3 fatty acids in organic milk, holding across seasons, and one of 67 studies found 47% more in organic meat, with very high heterogeneity and low reliability. Organic crops carry modestly more phenolic compounds, 14 to 26% for total phenolics in published meta-analyses and more for some subgroups, though subgroup estimates are less reliable. The reviewers say these differences are not a sufficient basis for conclusions about health, and dairy and meat are a minor source of omega-3 in most diets.

arc.hook: Put organic and conventional milk side by side and ask what is actually different inside.
arc.conflict: The claims pulling in different directions: "Organic food is more nutritious than conventional food"; "Organic crops contain more antioxidants and polyphenols than conventional crops"; "Organic milk and meat contain more omega-3 fatty acids than conventional milk and meat"; "Eating organic food has proven health benefits for the people who eat it"; "Eating organic food lowers cancer risk"; "Organic buyers are wealthier and healthier, which confounds studies of organic diets and health"; "Eating more fruit and vegetables matters more than whether they are organic".
arc.evidence: Each claim's verdict, strongest study first.
arc.resolution: Organic milk has clearly more omega-3, organic crops modestly more polyphenols; whether that changes anyone's health is not shown.
arc.takeaway: A decision rule the viewer can apply.

coherence.explanation: Pruned to one question, is organic food more nutritious, answered by the two composition differences the meta-analyses establish (polyphenols in crops, omega-3 in milk and meat). Health outcomes, cancer and confounding are their own chained story; the blanket 'more nutritious' claim is contradicted and stays out, and the fruit-and-vegetables claim has no deciding study.

stories.title: Does Organic Food Lower Your Cancer Risk?
alternates: Two Big Studies, Two Answers on Organic Food and Cancer
The 25% Cancer Headline, Read Closely
stories.question: Does eating organic food lower your risk of cancer?
stories.whyWatch: A 2018 French study made headlines with 25% fewer cancers among organic eaters, while a far larger UK study found no overall effect. Putting them side by side shows what an observational study can and cannot tell you.
stories.tension: NutriNet-Sante found a 25% lower cancer hazard in its most organic quartile; the Million Women Study, with nine times the participants and twice the follow-up, found none overall. Both agree on one cancer, and both studied people whose habits differ in other ways.
stories.evidenceNeeded: The two large prospective cohorts compared on size, follow-up and adjustment, a systematic review placing them together, and data on how organic eaters differ from other people.

stories.premise: The evidence does not show that organic food lowers cancer risk. In 623,080 UK women followed 9.3 years, usually or always eating organic was not linked to lower total cancer (RR 1.03) and breast cancer was slightly higher; only non-Hodgkin lymphoma was lower, which the authors say may be chance. In 68,946 French adults followed 4.6 years, the most organic quartile had a 25% lower hazard of any cancer, an absolute difference of 0.6%, mainly for lymphomas and postmenopausal breast cancer. Both are observational: the French organic eaters were more often higher-income, educated, active and plant-eating, and the UK ones exercised more and smoked less, though income differed little there. Residual confounding is the likeliest reading of the split; lymphoma is the one signal both share.

arc.takeaway: The conditions under which the claim holds, instead of a yes or no.
